anchor.context: Artificial muscles are a key enabling technology for this class of robot. Among the available actuation technologies, McKibben-style braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) combine low mass, high force-to-weight ratio, and intrinsic compliance with a force--length curve that qualitatively resembles that of skeletal muscle \citep{liang_comparative_2020, hunt_modeling_2017}. BPAs have been used in quadrupedal robots \citep{aschenbeck_design_2006, hunt_modeling_2017, scharzenberger_design_2019}, musculoskeletal humanoids \citep{asano_design_2017, hitzmann_anthropomorphic_2018}, and dexterous manipulation systems \citep{chen_realizing_2019}. However, BPAs also differ from biological muscle in important ways: their maximum tensile force occurs at resting length rather than at an optimal fiber length, their maximum contraction ratio is substantially lower than that of human muscle, and their force output is a highly nonlinear function of internal pressure, contraction, and loading state \citep{hunt_modeling_2017, sarosi_comparative_2017, liang_comparative_2020}. My experience with \qty{10}{\mm} actuators made this gap concrete: manufacturer specifications overstate the force and contraction available at the short resting lengths a leg design requires, and designs based on those specifications delivered less range of motion and joint torque than intended. Nor could the published empirical models fill in the gaps, because each is fitted to measurements at a single resting length \citep{sarosi_comparative_2017, martens_modeling_2017, hunt_modeling_2017}; none accurately predicts how force changes when a designer chooses a different actuator length. anchor.text: Two definitions cover most of the neuroscience vocabulary used below. First, the locomotor controller is a two-level central pattern generator: a rhythm generator sets the timing of the step cycle, and a pattern-formation layer shapes that timing into phase-appropriate activation of antagonist muscle groups \citep{rybak_modelling_2006}. Each leg's rhythm generator is a pair of mutually inhibiting antagonist populations, one extensor and one flexor, so that only one is strongly active at a time. Second, in the non-spiking (graded) formulation used for most of this work, each neuron is electrically a nonlinear RC circuit: synaptic current charges a membrane capacitance through a leak conductance, and the resulting membrane voltage, tens of millivolts, is both the neuron's state and its output \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Graded chemical synapses couple these units: a depolarized presynaptic cell opens a conductance in the postsynaptic membrane whose sign makes the connection excitatory or inhibitory. edit.original: Three published circuits, reproduced in Figures~\ref{fig:deng_connectome}, \ref{fig:afferent_connectomes}, and~\ref{fig:shinohara_connectome}, place these afferent channels in their circuit context. The rat hindlimb controller of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} is organized exactly as Section~\ref{sec:bg_neural} describes: a rhythm-generator half-center and a pattern-formation layer sit above a sensory--motor network in which extensor and flexor muscle receptors feed back through interneurons and Renshaw cells onto the same motoneurons the CPG drives. The human-scale model of \citet{dirusso_investigating_2023} carries the idea to a full lower limb: each agonist--antagonist muscle pair carries Ia, II, and Ib reflex populations with Renshaw cells, and pattern-formation nodes from the locomotor controller terminate on the same motoneuron pools. The cat interlimb model of \citet{shinohara_mechanisms_2025} adds the left--right half of the problem, coupling the two rhythm generators through V3 and commissural interneuron populations while force, length, and velocity feedback returns from every muscle. The schematics differ in animal, scale, and emphasis, but they wire the same afferent classes of this section into the circuit at the level each hypothesis concerns, whether that is the rhythm generator, the pattern-formation layer, or the motor pool. \begin{figure}[htbp] \centering \includegraphics[width=1.0\textwidth]{deng_cpg_connectome.pdf} % ALT TEXT: A four-panel circuit schematic: single-limb control hierarchy, % rhythm-generator configuration, pattern-formation network, and a % sensory-motor network with extensor and flexor receptors, interneurons, % Renshaw cells, motoneurons, and muscles. \caption[Deng two-layer CPG and sensory--motor network]{Synthetic nervous system of the rat hindlimb model: \textbf{(A)} single limb control hierarchy, \textbf{(B)} rhythm-generator configuration, \textbf{(C)} pattern-formation network, and \textbf{(D)} sensory--motor network. anchor.context: For robots, these biological architectures can be implemented as synthetic nervous systems (SNSs): networks of conductance-based spiking and non-spiking neurons that are small enough to run in real time yet biologically grounded enough to be compared against animal data. anchor.context: Artificial muscles are a key enabling technology for this class of robot. Among the available actuation technologies, McKibben-style braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) combine low mass, high force-to-weight ratio, and intrinsic compliance with a force--length curve that qualitatively resembles that of skeletal muscle \citep{liang_comparative_2020, hunt_modeling_2017}. BPAs have been used in quadrupedal robots \citep{aschenbeck_design_2006, hunt_modeling_2017, scharzenberger_design_2019}, musculoskeletal humanoids \citep{asano_design_2017, hitzmann_anthropomorphic_2018}, and dexterous manipulation systems \citep{chen_realizing_2019}. However, BPAs also differ from biological muscle in important ways: their maximum tensile force occurs at resting length rather than at an optimal fiber length, their maximum contraction ratio is substantially lower than that of human muscle, and their force output is a highly nonlinear function of internal pressure, contraction, and loading state \citep{hunt_modeling_2017, sarosi_comparative_2017, liang_comparative_2020}. My experience with \qty{10}{\mm} actuators made this gap concrete: manufacturer specifications overstate the force and contraction available at the short resting lengths a leg design requires, and designs based on those specifications delivered less range of motion and joint torque than intended. Nor could the published empirical models fill in the gaps, because each is fitted to measurements at a single resting length \citep{sarosi_comparative_2017, martens_modeling_2017, hunt_modeling_2017}; none accurately predicts how force changes when a designer chooses a different actuator length. Because muscle resting length is one of the primary degrees of freedom available to the robot designer, the absence of a force model valid at arbitrary resting length blocked accurate actuator selection. Designing a biomimetic robot around BPAs therefore requires quantitative, predictive models of the actuator and of the joint torques it can produce.

anchor.context: Sensory feedback is not a passive correction layer but an integral part of locomotor pattern generation. Reviews of afferent control of the CPG \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998} and of muscle proprioceptive feedback and spinal networks \citep{windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022} summarize the classical picture: group Ia afferents from muscle spindles signal muscle length and velocity, group Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs signal force, and group II afferents signal length, with load-related feedback playing a role distinct from length-related feedback during locomotion \citep{dietz_significance_2000}. Removing proprioceptive feedback degrades locomotor patterns in mice \citep{akay_degradation_2014}; proprioceptive input regulates and adapts locomotor activity \citep{lam_role_2002}; and the relative contributions of proprioceptive and vestibular systems to locomotion are the subject of ongoing study \citep{akay_relative_2021, akay_sensory_2020}. Tonic central and sensory stimuli have been shown to facilitate involuntary air-stepping in humans \citep{selionov_tonic_2009}, demonstrating that simple graded stimulation of motoneuronal and rhythmic circuits can elicit stepping-like output, an experiment readily reproduced in simulation by tonic stimulation of pattern-formation and rhythm-generator populations. The proprioceptive and contact feedback channels designed in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} follow this afferent organization.

anchor.context: Neuromechanical simulation, the coupling of a musculoskeletal model to a model of the neural controller that drives it, has advanced along three partially overlapping lines. The first line embeds reflex physiology directly into the controller. The muscle-reflex walking model of \citet{geyer_musclereflex_2010} demonstrated that positive force, length, and velocity feedback around each muscle, organized with simple interlimb coordination, is sufficient to produce self-stabilizing human-like walking dynamics and realistic muscle activations without any central pattern generator. That model became the reference point for a generation of reflex-based neuromechanical controllers, including the cat hindlimb models of Section~\ref{sec:bg_compneuro} \citep{markin_afferent_2010, shevtsova_modeling_2016} and their extensions. Hybrid work makes the complementarity of the two strategies explicit: \citet{haeufle_benefit_2018} combined feed-forward muscle activations with neuronal reflex feedback in simulated human walking and found that the robustness benefit of each depends on which muscle carries it.

anchor.context: The experiments this research program is designed to enable, including deleting a muscle from a limb, blocking a sensory pathway, lesioning part of a rhythm generator, and applying tonic stimulation to spinal circuits, cannot be performed on healthy humans. Invasive intervention on the human neuromuscular system is limited to clinical populations, is tightly constrained by ethics review, and permits neither the within-subject control nor the reversibility that neuromechanical hypotheses demand. The same experiments in animals also carry real moral cost, and their justification is governed by the Three Rs framework: replacement of animal subjects with non-animal methods, reduction of the numbers required, and refinement of the remaining procedures \citep{russell_principles_1959, tannenbaum_russell_2015}. A robot that implements a validated neuromechanical hypothesis is precisely such a replacement method: every deletion, lesion, and stimulation experiment that runs on the synthetic nervous system is an experiment that does not require a living subject, and the robot population can be duplicated exactly, so that ``subjects'' are statistically identical across conditions, an experimental repeatability no breeding colony can offer. The failure modes of these experiments damage hardware, not tissue.
